scenes.narration: One gram of activated sludge holds tens of billions of living bacteria.
scenes.title: SEWAGE IS A BACTERIA FARM

scenes.narration: A wastewater plant is not really a filter; it is a bacteria farm.
In 1914, Ardern and Lockett in Manchester aerated sewage and reused the sludge.
Blowers pump in air, and bacteria clump into flocs that eat the pollution. In the clarifier, heavy flocs settle and treated water flows off the top.
With oxygen, nitrifying bacteria convert toxic ammonia into nitrate. Without oxygen, other bacteria turn that nitrate into harmless nitrogen gas.
Sludge age is about 5 to 15 days, long enough for slow nitrifiers.
scenes.caption: 5–15 DAYS

scenes.narration: US law demands 85 percent removal of organic pollution; good plants reach 95.
Blowing that air is the biggest energy cost, often around half the total.
Honestly, waste never truly vanishes; it becomes gas, water and surplus sludge.
scenes.caption: NOT DELETED

scenes.narration: The real engineering is building a home where the right microbes can thrive. Follow for more.

sources.claim: Activated sludge holds ~3.0x10^10 viable (culturable) cells per gram of mixed-liquor solids (2.8x10^7 per mL); culture-based, so a floor. Older plate counts: several hundred thousand million per gram.

Ardern and Lockett presented activated sludge to the Society of Chemical Industry in Manchester on 3 April 1914; key insight was returning settled biomass; work done at Davyhulme.
